title: The Best U.S. Brokerages for Long-Term, Low-Fee Index Investing
description: Fidelity vs. Vanguard vs. Schwab: Choosing your wealth home.
content:
If you want to build wealth, you need a brokerage account. But not all platforms are built for long-term investors. Some apps (like Robinhood) are designed to make you trade frequently, which destroys wealth. Others (like Vanguard) are designed to be boring vaults where money grows for decades. Choosing the right 'Container' for your money is as important as the investment itself. This guide compares the 'Big 3' US brokerages on fees, features, and user experience for the buy-and-hold investor.

Key Takeaways

  • Zero Is Standard: All major US brokers now offer $0 stock/ETF trades. Do not pay commissions.
  • The Cash Sweep Difference: This is the hidden differentiator. Fidelity pays ~5% on uninvested cash. Schwab pays ~0.4%. On $10k cash, Fidelity pays you $460/yr more.
  • Fractional Shares: Fidelity allows you to buy $1 of any stock or ETF. Schwab only allows S&P 500 stocks. Vanguard allows almost none (except their own ETFs). Fidelity wins for small accounts.
  • Mutual Fund Access: If you want to automate investing (e.g., $500/mo auto-invest), Mutual Funds are better than ETFs. Each broker prefers their own funds (Fidelity Funds at Fidelity, etc.).

Why It Matters (US Context)

SIPC Insurance ($500k protection) covers all these brokers. The safety is identical. The choice comes down to UX and features.

The Scorecard

Ranking the best homes for your IRA.

1. Fidelity (The Winner)

  • Best Feature: SPAXX (Core Position). Your cash automatically earns 5% without you doing anything.
  • Cost: Offers 'Zero Expense Ratio' funds (FZROX) with 0.00% fees.
  • UX: Functional but dense.
  • Verdict: The best all-around platform for maximizing every penny.

2. Charles Schwab (The Runner Up)

  • Best Feature: Banking. The Investor Checking card refunds all ATM fees globally.
  • Weakness: Cash sweep pays almost nothing (0.45%). You must manually buy a money market fund (SWVXX) to get yield.
  • Verdict: Best if you want to combine banking and investing.

3. Vanguard (The Old Guard)

  • Best Feature: Client-owned structure. Incentives are aligned with you.
  • Weakness: The app/website is outdated and clunky. No fractional ETFs.
  • Verdict: Good for people who want to log in once a year and never be tempted to trade.

How to Switch

  1. Don't Sell: You do not need to sell your stocks to switch brokers. Use an 'ACATS' transfer. The new broker pulls your assets over 'In-Kind' (as they are). No taxes triggered.
  2. Fee Reimbursement: The old broker usually charges $75 to leave. The new broker (Fidelity/Schwab) will usually reimburse this fee if you ask. Never pay to switch.
  3. Consolidate: Having an IRA at Vanguard, a 401k at Fidelity, and a Taxable account at Robinhood is messy. Moving everything to one login simplifies your life and makes tracking Net Worth easier.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Robinhood good for long term?

It's getting better (IRA Match is great), but the app is designed to trigger dopamine. If you have self-control, it's fine. If you are tempted to gamble, stick to Fidelity.

What about M1 Finance?

Great for 'Pie' investing (automation). But customer service is weaker than the Big 3. Good for intermediate investors who want strict allocation control.

Can I buy Vanguard funds at Fidelity?

Yes. You can buy Vanguard ETFs (VTI) at Fidelity for free. But if you buy Vanguard Mutual Funds (VTSAX) at Fidelity, there is a $75 fee. Stick to ETFs if crossing brokers.
